Chastise
chas-TIZE
v.
From Old French chastier, from Latin castigare: castus (pure) + agere (to make, drive)—literally to make pure. Correction aimed at cleansing, not at venting.

Biblical Definition

Chastise is corrective discipline administered by an authority who loves the one corrected and intends his good. The etymology—to make pure—is the biblical sense exactly. Hebrews states the doctrine plainly: whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth (Heb 12:6), and then turns the argument in a direction the modern reader rarely expects: if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons (Heb 12:8). The absence of correction is not evidence of favor but of no relationship at all. Fathers are commanded into the same office: he that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes (Prov 13:24)—and betimes matters, meaning early, before the fault hardens. God chastises corporately too: I, even I, will chastise you seven times for your sins (Lev 26:28), the covenant curses functioning as escalating discipline meant to drive a people back rather than merely to punish them. Scripture is careful about the shape of it. Chastisement is measured, purposeful, temporary, administered by one with the right to administer it, and aimed at holiness—that we might be partakers of his holiness (Heb 12:10). It is neither abuse (which is rage using discipline as cover) nor indulgence (which is the withholding Proverbs calls hatred). Even Pilate's cynical I will therefore chastise him, and release him (Luke 23:16) borrows the vocabulary of correction to describe a scourging with no righteous purpose in it at all.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CHASTISE as to correct by punishment; to punish for the purpose of reclaiming an offender; to inflict pain for the purpose of correction or reformation.

expand to see more

CHASTISE, v.t. — To correct by punishing; to punish; to inflict pain by stripes, or in other manner, for the purpose of punishing an offender and recalling him to his duty. I will chastise you seven times for your sins (Lev 26:28).

CHASTISE, v.t. — To reduce to order or obedience; to restrain; to awe; to correct. Hence, to purify, as by discipline.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 12:6 — "For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth."

Hebrews 12:8 — "But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons."

Proverbs 13:24 — "He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes."

Leviticus 26:28 — "Then I will walk contrary unto you also in fury; and I, even I, will chastise you seven times for your sins."

Modern Corruption

The age has collapsed chastisement into abuse at one end and permissiveness at the other, treating all corrective pain as trauma—so that Hebrews 12, which calls the absence of chastening a mark of bastardy, has become nearly unreadable.

expand to see more

The dominant corruption identifies all discipline with violence. Any imposed consequence is reframed as harm done to a developing self, and correction is replaced with negotiation, accommodation, or referral. There is a real abuse the church must name and refuse: rage that calls itself correction, punishment that serves the punisher, discipline unmoored from love and proportion. Scripture condemns that as loudly as anyone, forbidding fathers to provoke their children to wrath. But it condemns the opposite too, and with a sharper word: the father who spares the rod hateth his son. Withholding correction is not gentleness; Proverbs classifies it as hatred, because it abandons a child to his own folly.

The second corruption runs the other way and is common in religious homes: chastisement as temper with a verse attached. The biblical form is measured, early (betimes), explained, and aimed at holiness rather than at compliance or at the parent's relief. Hebrews 12:10 supplies the test—earthly fathers chastened after their own pleasure, but God for our profit. Any correction that serves the corrector's pleasure has already left the biblical category, whatever text is quoted over it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yasar, to discipline or instruct by correction; Greek paideuō, to train a child—the verb behind Hebrews 12 and the root of pedagogy.

expand to see more

Hebrew yasar (H3256) — to chasten, discipline, instruct; the noun musar is the instruction Proverbs urges a son to receive (Deut 8:5; Prov 13:24; 19:18; Lev 26:28).

Greek paideuō (G3811) — to train or instruct a child, hence to chastise as part of upbringing; the whole argument of Hebrews 12:5-11 (Eph 6:4; 2 Tim 3:16; Titus 2:12).

Greek mastigoō (G3146) — to scourge; the intensifying verb of Hebrews 12:6, scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.

Usage

"Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth—correction is evidence of sonship, not of rejection."

"If ye be without chastisement... then are ye bastards, and not sons—Hebrews 12:8 inverts the modern instinct."

"Proverbs 13:24 calls the withholding of the rod hatred, and requires it betimes—early."
